--- title: "Measurement error" subtitle: "Can it help detect ascertainment bias?" description: "Critical analysis of a recent unblinded RCT from the NEJM" author: - name: Jay Brophy url: https://brophyj.github.io/ orcid: 0000-0001-8049-6875 affiliation: McGill University Dept Medicine, Epidemiology & Biostatistics affiliation-url: https://mcgill.ca categories: [Measurement error, RCTs, biases] image: preview-image.png citation: url: https://brophyj.com/posts/2026-11-09-unblinded/ date: 2026-11-09 lastmod: 2026-11-09 featured: true draft: false projects: [] format: html: theme: [simple, ../../custom.scss] code-fold: true code-tools: true embed-resources: true toc: true execute: warning: false message: false --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) ``` ::: ## Background On November 8 2026, the NEJM published ["Left Bundle-Branch Pacing versus Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block"](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2612972?query=featured_home). This open-label, randomized, controlled trial assigned patients with atrioventricular block in a 1:1 ratio to receive left bundle-branch pacing or right ventricular pacing. The primary outcome was a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. At a median follow-up of 35.1 months (interquartile range, 23.6 to 40.7), the authors reported a primary-outcome event had occurred in 16 patients in the left bundle-branch pacing group and in 35 patients in the right ventricular pacing group (Kaplan–Meier 4-year cumulative incidence, 8.5% and 19.2%, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.41; 95% confidence interval, 0.23 to 0.75; P=0.003 by a stratified log-rank test). This lead the authors to conclude ::: callout-note ## Conclusion "*Among patients with atrioventricular block, left bundle-branch pacing was superior to right ventricular pacing in reducing the risk of a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.*" ::: ## Nuances to the conclusion The conclusion regarding the composite outcome certainly appears well supported by the reported data and statistical testing. However, the trial was [unblinded](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22371859/) and [stopped early](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20332404/), features associated with exaggerated effect estimates. This matters because deaths (15 vs. 13) and heart-failure hospitalizations (2 vs. 7 as first events) were both rare and similar and the benefit thus rests on a substantial increase in unblinded, adjudicated echocardiographic cardiomyopathy (0 vs. 19). Inconsistent with this, atrial fibrillation, stroke, 6-minute walk distance, quality of life, and NYHA class did not differ between the groups. Moreover, zero cardiomyopathy events, as defined as a drop in ejection fraction of at least 10 points to below 50%, among 342 LBBP patients is surprising as temporal variability of 2D ejection fraction can exceed [10 points](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23199515/). Simulating five protocol mandated follow-up echo-cardiograms per patient with a measurement SD of 4 points, measurement error alone would be expected to produce about five qualifying declines, even with no true change in ventricular function (Poisson probability of zero events ≈ 0.004). ::: {#tbl-sim .cell tbl-cap='Expected false-positive PICM events among 342 LBBP patients with perfectly stable true LVEF, by echo measurement SD (5000 simulations each)'} ```{.r .cell-code} ## How surprising are 0 pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM) events ## among 342 LBBP patients (OptimPacing, NEJM 2026)? ## ## Question: if every patient's TRUE ejection fraction were perfectly stable, ## how many would still meet the PICM echo definition through measurement ## variability alone? ## PICM definition: decrease >= 10 points from post-implant baseline, ## with resulting LVEF < 50%. ## Protocol (Table 1): pre-discharge baseline echo + 5 follow-up echoes ## (3, 6, 12, 24, 36 months). set.seed(2026) n <- 342 # LBBP patients n_fu <- 5 # follow-up echoes per protocol ef_mu <- 63.2 # baseline mean LVEF, LBBP arm (Table 1) ef_sd <- 5.9 # observed baseline SD (includes measurement error) nsim <- 5000 sim_noise <- function(sd_meas) { sd_true <- sqrt(ef_sd^2 - sd_meas^2) # true between-patient SD ev <- replicate(nsim, { ef_true <- rnorm(n, ef_mu, sd_true) # true EF base <- ef_true + rnorm(n, 0, sd_meas) # baseline = true + error fu <- ef_true + matrix(rnorm(n * n_fu, 0, sd_meas), n, n_fu) # 342 x 5 follow-up measurements sum(apply((base - fu >= 10) & (fu < 50), 1, any)) }) lambda <- mean(ev) # expected number of false events c(sd_meas = sd_meas, p_per_patient = lambda / n, expected_events = lambda, P0_simulated = mean(ev == 0), P0_poisson = exp(-lambda)) # Poisson P(0) = exp(-lambda) } res <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(c(3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5), sim_noise))) kable(signif(res, 3), col.names = c("Measurement SD", "P(event) per patient", "Expected events", "P(0 events), simulated", "P(0 events), Poisson")) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Measurement SD P(event) per patient Expected events P(0 events), simulated P(0 events), Poisson
3.0 0.00376 1.29 0.2810 2.76e-01
3.5 0.00870 2.97 0.0552 5.11e-02
4.0 0.01590 5.42 0.0054 4.41e-03
4.5 0.02420 8.28 0.0002 2.54e-04
5.0 0.03300 11.30 0.0000 1.24e-05
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Preview image for the blog listing: must be a ggplot object, saved ## relative to this post's folder (Quarto renders from the post's directory) p_prev <- ggplot(res, aes(sd_meas, expected_events)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") + annotate("text", x = 3, y = 0.4, hjust = 0, colour = "firebrick", label = "Observed in LBBP arm: 0 events") + labs(x = "Echo measurement SD (LVEF points)", y = "Expected false PICM events (n = 342)", title = "Events expected from echo measurement error alone") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ggsave("preview-image.png", p_prev, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 150, bg = "white") ## Note: a 2D-echo temporal variability >10 points (Thavendiranathan et al., ## JACC 2013) corresponds to a per-measurement SD of roughly 3.5-5 points. ## Any true intercurrent decline (ischemia, AF, valve disease) would only add ## events, so these probabilities of zero are upper bounds. ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_prev ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Expected number of false-positive PICM events from measurement error alone](index_files/figure-html/preview-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Differential ascertainment or adjudication therefore seems a plausible explanation. A trial with blinded adjudication and clinical end points would seem needed. ## Lessons I wrote this up in a Letter to the NEJM, although their 175 word format means it is impossible to articulate the fill content of this blog and explains why I bothered with this post. Yet another reason is my NEJM letters' acceptance rate is probably less than one in five. 1. **Composite endpoints** increase statistical power but with different health impacts the individual components should also be examined 2. **Unblinded** assessments of of judgmental (soft) outcomes may be subject to unintended ascertainment bias 3. **Measurement** error is a fact of clinical research and should not be overlooked. Here measurement error paradoxically provided additional support for the existence of ascertainment bias.
